report:
Based on the evidence, here is my conclusion.

**Bottom line: No — well-conducted trials show CoQ10 does not meaningfully improve Parkinson's disease movement (motor) symptoms.**

Early interest in CoQ10 came from its role in mitochondrial energy production and antioxidant defense, both implicated in Parkinson's disease pathology. Small, earlier-phase studies suggested a possible modest slowing of disability progression, prompting a large, definitive phase III trial.

The **QE3 trial** (Parkinson Study Group, published in *JAMA Neurology*, 2014) was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study testing high-dose (1,200 mg/day and 2,400 mg/day) CoQ10 versus placebo in early, untreated PD. It was stopped early for futility — the higher dose showed no benefit and there was no signal that continuing would show benefit on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), the standard measure of motor and functional disability (jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409; michaeljfox.org/news/coenzyme-q10-study-shows-no-clinical-benefit).

A separate randomized, placebo-controlled trial using nanoparticular CoQ10 (100 mg three times daily) in PD patients without motor fluctuations over three months likewise found no significant improvement (jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/794066).

A more recent systematic review (Mendes Sanchez et al., *Journal of Personalized Medicine/MDPI*, 2022) examining CoQ10 in Parkinsonian syndromes confirms that while PD patients often have lower CoQ10 levels, supplementation trials have consistently failed to demonstrate clinical benefit on motor symptoms or disease progression (mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975).

**Conclusion:** Despite biological plausibility and early promise, rigorous randomized trials—including a large phase III futility trial—found no evidence that CoQ10 supplementation improves movement symptoms or slows progression in Parkinson's disease. It is not recommended as a treatment for PD motor symptoms.
